en: In that regard, what is the formal establishment of the designation of affliction (*saṃkleśaprajñaptivyavasthāna*)?

It should be understood through three types of affliction. What, then, are they? They are the affliction of defilements (*kleśasaṃkleśa*), the affliction of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*), and the affliction of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*).
What is the affliction of defilements? The summary verse (*uddāna*) is as follows:
Its intrinsic nature, its classifications, its causes, its stages, its aspects, as well as its gravity, its perversion, its synonyms, and its faults.

The nature (*svabhāva*) of the afflictive obscuration (*kleśasaṃkleśa*) should be understood; its classification (*prabheda*), cause (*hetu*), state (*avasthā*), gateway (*mukha*), intensity (*adhimātratā*), inclusion of errors (*viparyāsasaṃgraha*), synonyms (*paryāya*), and disadvantage (*ādīnava*) should also be understood.
What is the nature of the afflictions?

That phenomenon which, when arising, arises with a non-peaceful characteristic (*apraśāntalakṣaṇa*) of its own accord, and through whose arising the continuum of conditioned formations (*saṃskārasantati*) proceeds in a state of non-peace—this should be understood as the complete nature of the afflictions.
What is the classification of the afflictions (*kleśa*)? [1] They may be of one kind: by way of being the defilement of affliction (*kleśasaṃkleśa*).
[2] They may be of two kinds: those to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*).
It may be threefold: associated with the desire realm, associated with the form realm, and associated with the formless realm.

It may be fourfold: associated with the desire realm and either specified or unspecified; associated with the form realm and unspecified; and associated with the formless realm and unspecified. It may be fivefold: to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, to be abandoned by the vision of origin, to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, to be abandoned by the vision of the path, and to be abandoned by cultivation.
It may be sixfold: attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

It may be sevenfold: the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmārāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of view (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).
It may be eightfold: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, view, and the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*).

It may be of nine kinds: the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), namely: the fetter of attachment (*anunaya*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of clinging to views (*parāmarśa*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*).

It may be of ten kinds: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

There may be one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*), based on the classification of these same ten afflictions according to their misapprehension of the twelve aspects of the truths (*satya*). What are the twelve aspects of the truths?

They are: the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The truth of cessation and the truth of the path that have the desire realm as their dominant condition, which are the fruit of the full comprehension of that [realm] and are produced by the full comprehension of that—[likewise] the truth of cessation and the truth of the path that have the form realm as their dominant condition, which are the fruit of the full comprehension of that and are produced by the full comprehension of that; and the truth of cessation and the truth of the path that have the formless realm as their dominant condition, which are the fruit of the full comprehension of that and are produced by the full comprehension of that.

Regarding these, all ten afflictions are in opposition to the truth of suffering and the truth of origin pertaining to the desire realm, as well as to the truth of cessation and the truth of the path that have the desire realm as their dominant condition.

In the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), with respect to the truth of suffering, the truth of origin, and the truths of cessation and the path which have those as their dominant influence, those same ten afflictions (*kleśa*)—excluding hostility (*pratigha*)—are the ones erroneously directed toward them. As it is in the realm of form, so it is in the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).

Regarding the cultivation that serves as the antidote to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), six afflictions are erroneously directed toward it, excluding false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Regarding the cultivation of the antidote to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), five afflictions (*kleśa*) are erroneous; these are derived from the same six [afflictions], excluding hostility (*pratigha*).
Just as it is with the antidote to the form realm, so it is with the antidote to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Just as they are erroneous, so too are they obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).
In that regard, what is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

It is [the view] arising from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing the false dharma, improper mental attention, or the natural loss of mindfulness; it consists in regarding the five aggregates of clinging as a self or as belonging to a self.
Or, for one who views [them] thus, it is that afflicted wisdom which is either determinate or indeterminate.
What is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
It arises based on association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*).

Or again, it is innate forgetfulness of mindfulness; it is that afflicted wisdom— whether determined or undetermined— which views the five aggregates of clinging as a self, or views them as eternal or as subject to annihilation.

[3] What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? It is that afflicted wisdom which is definitively determined, arising from associating with unwholesome persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention, whereby one either denies the cause, the fruit, or the efficacy of action, or destroys an existing entity.
[4] What is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?

Based on association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention, there is that afflicted wisdom which—having taken as its basis the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), together with their bases, objects, causes, co-existent factors, and associated mental states—and having compared them with other views, regards them as foremost, best, distinguished, and supreme; this is the afflicted wisdom that is definitively determined.
[5] What is the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

Based upon association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention, that which is the very view, along with the morality or vow that follows that view—along with its basis, its object, its cause, and its concomitant associated factors—which one regards as purity, liberation, and the means of deliverance: such is the definitively determined, afflicted wisdom.
What is attachment?
It is based upon association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention.
Or it is innate forgetfulness of mindfulness (*smṛti-sampramoṣa*), which is the attachment to a desired object, whether external or internal, determined or undetermined.
What is resistance (*pratigha*)?

Based on association with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention, or natural loss of mindfulness, there arises— whether directed externally or internally, whether determined or undetermined— an aversion toward undesirable objects.
What is pride (*māna*)? It is that which,
based on associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*),
or natural loss of mindfulness, is determined either externally or internally.
It is the inflation [of pride] regarding the high and low or the inferior and superior, whether [the object] is determined or undetermined.
What is ignorance?

It is the afflicted lack of knowledge regarding a knowable object—whether determined or undetermined—arising from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, improper mental attention, or natural loss of mindfulness.
What is doubt?

It is the state of indecision regarding an object of knowledge that has already been determined, arising from associating with unworthy persons, hearing false teachings, and improper mental attention.
What is the cause of the afflictions?

There are six causes: affliction arises from the basis (*āśraya*), from the object (*ālambana*), from association (*saṃsarga*), from teaching (*deśanā*), from habituation (*abhyāsa*), and from mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Among these, "from the basis" refers to that which arises as a latent disposition (*anuśaya*) and so forth.
Among these, "from the object" refers to when an object conducive to affliction has come into range.
In that regard, [it arises] through association: for one who follows the example of bad persons; through teaching: for one who hears the false dharma;
and through habituation: for one due to the force of previous familiarity.
In that regard, [the state arising] from mental attention (*manasikāra*) is that which arises for one who attends to things in an improper manner (*ayoniśas*).
How many states of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are there? In brief, there are seven:

the state of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the state of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the state of the imagined (*parikalpita*), the state of the innate (*sahaja*), the weak state, the medium state, and the intense state.
In that regard, the latent tendency of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) lies dormant due to two causes:
by way of the persistence of the seed and by way of its predominance.
Through how many aspects do the afflictions bring about defilement?
In brief, it is by way of two aspects:
[a] by way of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and [b] by way of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). [a] How is it by way of the outbursts?

In five ways: by way of dwelling in a state that is not peaceful; by way of being an obstacle to the wholesome; by way of giving rise to misconduct leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*); by way of embracing loss in this very life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika-jyāni*); and by way of producing the sufferings of birth and so forth.
[b] How does it defile by way of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)? By way of providing a basis for the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and by way of producing the sufferings of birth and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that all afflictions (*kleśa*), which act as obstacles to vision and cultivation, function as hindrances through seven aspects:

namely, through wrong comprehension, non-comprehension, both comprehension and non-comprehension, practice based on wrong comprehension, the basis and ground for those [afflictions], the production of terror by them, and their natural habitual manifestation.
How is an affliction to be understood as having the characteristic of being excessive, intense, or heavy?

In brief, there are six aspects: by way of the offense (*āpatti*), the rebirth (*upapatti*), the continuum (*saṃtāna*), the object (*vastu*), the origination of the action (*karma-samutthāna*), and the limit (*paryanta*).
Among these, the offense is that state of obsession with afflictions (*kleśāparyavasthāna*) by which one incurs an offense without remainder.
Among these, rebirth is that which belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) or that which leads to the states of woe (*apāyika*).

In that regard, [it is] from the perspective of the continuum (*saṃtāna*): that which belongs to those who are characterized by passion and so forth, whose faculties are matured, who are young, and who do not possess the nature of attaining final nirvāṇa.

In that regard, from the perspective of the object (*vastu*): that which has as its objective support a field of respect (*guru-kṣetra*), a field of qualities (*guṇa-kṣetra*), or an unapproachable field (*agamya-kṣetra*).

In that regard, from the perspective of the origination of action (*karmasamutthāna*): that which one initiates as bodily or vocal action when one is neither overwhelmed nor completely consumed by the obsession of the afflictions (*kleśaparyavasthāna*).
In that regard, from the perspective of the ultimate limit: that which is comprised of the highest degree by its very nature is abandoned first by means of the weak counteragent.
These are the seven distortions (*viparyāsa*):

namely, distortion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), distortion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), distortion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), the distortion of [perceiving] the permanent in the impermanent, the distortion of [perceiving] pleasure in suffering, the distortion of [perceiving] the pure in the impure, and the distortions of [perceiving] a self in what is not-self.

What is the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*)? It is the conceptual constructions of perception that take the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be happiness, the impure to be pure, and the non-self to be self.

What is the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*)? It is the acceptance, approval, establishment, and dogmatic attachment toward that very thing which has been thus conceptually constructed by perception.
What is the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*)? It is the affliction of passion and so forth toward that very thing which has been thus dogmatically adhered to.
In this regard, the afflictions should be understood through three aspects:
there is an affliction that is the root of error, there is error itself, and there is the outflow of error.
Among these, the root of error is ignorance.

The perversions are: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a portion of the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and attachment (*rāga*).
The outflow of the perversions is: false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), a portion of the view of grasping at extremes, hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Among these, the view of a self-identity is the perversion of perceiving a self in what is not-self.
A portion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—namely, the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent—is [the first inversion].
The esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure.
The esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the inversion of perceiving suffering as happiness.
Attachment is twofold: it is the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure, and it is the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure. What is the synonym for the afflictions?

There are many synonyms [for the afflictions], namely: fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), graspings (*upādāna*), knots (*grantha*), hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), barrenness (*khila*), stains (*mala*), depravities (*nigha*), arrows (*śalya*), possessions (*kiṃcana*), roots (*mūla*), misconducts (*duścarita*), outflows (*āsrava*), vexations (*vighāta*), fevers (*paridāha*), desperations (*upāyāsa*), strifes (*raṇa*), fires (*agni*), fevers (*jvara*), forests (*vanasa*), and obstructions (*vinibandha*). Such are the categories of synonyms for the afflictions (*kleśa*). Among these, they are called "fetters" because they fetter one to suffering; they are called "bonds" because they prevent one from acting according to one's will in virtuous conduct.
They are called *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) because they follow along with all worldly excellence and noble birth;
they are called *upakleśas* (secondary afflictions) because they defile the mind through distortions (*viparyāsa*);
and they are called *paryavasthānas* (outbursts) because they manifest repeatedly.
They are called floods (*ogha*) because they are difficult to fathom and because they carry one away with the current.
They are called yokes (*yoga*) because they are the means for wrong practice. They are called grasping (*upādāna*) because they provide the continuity of personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
They are called "bonds" (*grantha*) because they are difficult to release; they are called "hindrances" (*nivaraṇa*) because they obscure the true meaning;
and they are called "barrennesses" (*khila*) because they are not a field for the growth of the crop of wholesome qualities.
They are *malas* (stains) because they are intrinsically defiled;
they are *nighas* (afflictions) because they constantly strike;
and they are *śalyas* (thorns) because their characteristic is lack of tranquility and because they have followed [the person] for a long time.

They are called "possessors" (*kiṃcana*) because they act as the cause for grasping at the substrata (*upadhi*). They are "deluded" (*mūḍha*) because they serve as the basis for unwholesome states. They are "evil conduct" (*duścarita*) because their intrinsic nature consists in wrong practice.
They are called *āsravas* because they cause the distraction of the mind; they are called *vighātas* because they produce dissatisfaction with enjoyments;
they are called *paridāhas* because they cause the frustration of desires.
They are called *upāyāsas* (afflictions) because they bring about misfortune;

they are called *raṇas* (battles) because they are the cause of quarreling, strife, contention, and burning; and they are called *agnayas* (fires) because they burn away the fuel of the accumulated roots of wholesome merit.
It is called *jvara* because it has become a great disease,
or because it destroys the trees of various forms of existence, or because it possesses the power of the qualities of desire.
They are called "obstructions" because they create obstacles to the attainment of supramundane dharmas.
These are synonyms for all the afflictions;
however, the Blessed One established those afflictions under various specific designations according to their predominance.
"Fetters" refers to the nine fetters: the fetter of attachment, and so forth, as detailed previously.
"Ties" refers to the three ties: lust, hatred, and delusion.
"Latent dispositions" refers to the seven latent dispositions: the latent disposition of sensual lust, and so forth, as detailed previously.
Regarding "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): there are three secondary afflictions, namely attachment, aversion, and delusion;
regarding "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*): there are eight envelopments, namely lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, torpor, restlessness, remorse, envy, and avarice.
"Floods" refers to the four floods: the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
As with the floods, so it is with the yokes (*yoga*).
"Graspings" refers to the four graspings: the grasping of sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*) and the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*).
The clinging to rules and observances is the clinging to the doctrine of self.

"Ties" refers to the four ties: the bodily tie of covetousness, the bodily tie of ill will, the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth.

"Hindrances" refers to the five hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
"Obstructions" (*khilāni*) refers to the three obstructions: passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
Just as there are obstructions, so too are there stains (*malāḥ*), hindrances (*nighāḥ*), thorns (*śalyāḥ*), possessions (*kiṃcanāḥ*), and misconducts (*duścaritāni*).
"Roots" (*mūlāni*) refers to the three roots: greed (*lobha*) is an unwholesome root; hatred and delusion are unwholesome roots.
The outflows (*āsrava*) are the three outflows: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).

The obstructions (*vighāta*) are the three obstructions: passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). Just as there are obstructions, so too are there torments (*paridāha*), despair (*upāyāsa*), afflictions (*varaṇa*), fires (*agni*), fevers (*jvara*), and forests (*vanasa*).

"Obstruction" refers to the five obstructions: dependence on the body, dependence on sensual pleasures, socializing with householders, lack of appropriate discourse, and contentment with only a small amount.
What is the disadvantage of the afflictions?
The manifold disadvantage should be understood as follows:
when a defilement arises, from the very beginning it defiles the mind and produces perversion regarding the object of focus.
It strengthens the underlying tendency;
it sets in motion a stream of formations that is a natural outflow;
it leads to harm for oneself, harm for others, and harm for both.
One incurs fault pertaining to the present life, fault pertaining to future lives, and fault pertaining to both the present and future lives.
One experiences the mental suffering and dejection born thereof,
and brings about the suffering of birth and so forth.
It distances the continuum from nirvāṇa; it causes one to fall away from wholesome dharmas;
and one encounters misfortune regarding enjoyments.
Being timid, lacking enthusiasm, and lacking confidence, he approaches the assembly.
A wicked report, dispraise, ill-repute, and a bad reputation spread in all directions and intermediate directions.
He becomes an object of reproach for the wise.
One dies with regret;
and after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in states of deprivation, miserable destinies, and perdition, in the hells;
and one does not attain one's own true welfare.
